analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to pay Medicaid-style rebates so states can give discount drug prices to uninsured residents.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in October 2002, sent to the Finance Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let every state set up a prescription drug discount program for residents who are uninsured or underinsured — Medicare beneficiaries and people earning up to 300% of the poverty line. Drug manufacturers would have to pay the same rebates to these state programs that they already pay under Medicaid, which average discounts of more than 40% off retail prices, and states with such programs would get extra rebates for their Medicaid programs. At least 95% of the rebate money would have to go directly to residents as lower drug prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 70 million Americans who lack adequate prescription drug coverage, including 18 million Medicare beneficiaries, would get access to the same rebated discounts states already receive through Medicaid. The bill cites Maine's 'Healthy Maine' program, which has served over 100,000 residents this way since June 2001, as the model to replicate nationwide [S3]. States would gain new federal rebate money with no requirement to spend their own funds [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and underinsured residents, especially seniors

how_it_helps.text: Extends Medicaid-level drug rebates to state discount programs covering Medicare beneficiaries and residents up to 300% of the poverty line, making discounted prices available to people who currently pay full retail [S3].
Requires that at least 95% of the rebates a state receives go to residents in the form of discounted prices, limiting how much can be absorbed elsewhere [S3].

Gives states that run discount programs enhanced rebates for their Medicaid programs — the federal government absorbs half the difference so the extra rebate does not reduce the state's Medicaid spending credit [S3].
States are not required to put up any of their own money, and amounts received cannot offset other Medicaid spending, making the program a federal rebate stream states can adopt at no cost [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the cost, paying rebates on drugs sold through state discount programs equal to what they pay under Medicaid rebate agreements — a condition for staying in the Medicaid rebate program at all [S2] [S3]. To the extent manufacturers offset that cost, it would be spread across their pricing, and taxpayers could share in it through Medicaid's enhanced rebate provision, which covers half the difference between the negotiated rebate and the standard formula [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill does not cap what manufacturers can charge at list price, so the discount depends entirely on the rebate mechanism; manufacturers could adjust their pricing behavior in response, and the bill contains no estimate of what the enhanced Medicaid rebate provision would cost the federal government [S3].
Eligibility is capped — only Medicare beneficiaries and residents up to 300% of the poverty line qualify, so uninsured residents above that income threshold would still pay full retail [S3].
States must opt in and run their own programs; residents of states that choose not to participate would get nothing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is clear: millions of people paying full retail for needed drugs would get discounts averaging over 40%, and states could offer this at no cost to their budgets. The cost falls on drug manufacturers, who would be compelled to pay rebates as a condition of Medicaid participation. The main design weaknesses are that coverage is means-tested and Medicare-limited rather than universal, states must opt in, and the enhanced Medicaid rebate provision quietly shifts some cost to the federal taxpayer.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-October 2002 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and Congress ended three months later without any vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Paul Wellstone introduced the bill on October 17, 2002, with Sens. Bingaman and Lincoln, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1] [S3] [S5].
The Finance Committee took no further action; the bill's action history ends with the referral, and it never reached the Senate floor [S5].
The bill was introduced less than three months before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, leaving no time for the committee to act [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, because they never had to pay rebates on drugs sold through state discount programs, and the more than 70 million uninsured and underinsured Americans the bill described got no discount from this route before the Congress ended [S3] [S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers, which avoided new rebate costs

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured its referral to the Finance Committee

for.name: Sens. Jeff Bingaman and Blanche Lincoln
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; 2 of 49 Senate Democrats signed on

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action; no markup or vote was ever held

against.name: Sen. Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: As the committee's chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; all three sponsors were Democrats, and the record shows no recorded opposition because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would force them to pay Medicaid-sized rebates on drugs sold through state discount programs, as a condition of keeping their Medicaid rebate agreements. Their interest in avoiding those rebates runs directly against uninsured patients paying full retail [S2] [S3].
States would receive a new rebate stream with no mandate to spend their own funds, and could extend discounted drugs to residents at essentially no budget cost [S3].
